subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Escalation of Commitment
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Escalation of Commitment.

hook.text: A company spent $50 million on a failing project. Instead of stopping, they approved another $30 million.

buildup.text: Escalation of commitment means increasing investment in a failing course of action to justify prior decisions.

discovery.text: Staw's research showed that decision-makers who felt responsible for the initial choice escalated the most.

twist.text: Bringing in a new decision-maker reduces escalation. Fresh eyes have no ego invested in the past choice.

climax.text: Set kill criteria before starting any project. Predetermined exit points remove ego from the stop decision.

punchline.text: Choose your exit point before the stakes rise.

quiz.question: What reduces escalation of commitment according to research?
options: Giving the original decision-maker more authority
Bringing in a new decision-maker with no ego in the past choice
Increasing the budget to show confidence

details.summary: Escalation of commitment is the tendency to continue investing in a failing course of action because of what has already been spent. People throw good money after bad, hoping to justify past investments and avoid admitting the initial decision was wrong.
details.whyItMatters: Escalation of commitment destroys value in business, government, and personal life by prolonging failing investments and projects. The desire to justify past decisions overrides the rational analysis of future prospects.
takeaways: Past investment creates psychological pressure to continue regardless of prospects
Escalation is driven by loss aversion, ego protection, and sunk cost reasoning
Setting pre-defined abandonment criteria before starting prevents escalation

faq.question: What is the most effective way to prevent escalation of commitment?
faq.answer: Before starting any project, define specific measurable criteria that would trigger cancellation. Having pre-committed kill criteria removes the emotional decision from the moment of truth, making abandonment a policy execution rather than an admission of failure.

faq.question: Why is escalation of commitment so common in organizations?
faq.answer: Decision-makers fear admitting their original judgment was wrong. Sunk costs feel like waste if abandoned. External constituencies and political pressures reward persistence over prudent withdrawal. The bias is structural, not just individual.
